terms.definition: The ratio of the loan amount requested or outstanding to the appraised value of the property securing the loan. Hard money lenders typically cap LTV lower than traditional banks (usually 60% to 75%) to offset risk.
terms.importance: Crucial metric for risk assessment. Traditional real estate uses current appraisal, while fix-and-flip scenarios prioritize ARV.

terms.definition: The ratio of the loan amount to the total cost of the acquisition and construction/renovation of a project. Hard money lenders frequently fund up to 80-90% of total project costs, provided the LTV/ARV limit is not exceeded.
terms.importance: Helps determine the amount of equity ('skin in the game') the borrower must personally inject into the deal.

terms.definition: A measurement of a property's available cash flow to pay its current debt obligations. While common in long-term rental or commercial hard money loans, it measures if net operating income can cover annual debt service.
terms.formula: DSCR = Net Operating Income (NOI) / Total Debt Service
terms.importance: A DSCR above 1.0 means positive cash flow. Most lenders require 1.15x to 1.25x for stabilized investment property loans.

terms.definition: The estimated future value of a property after all planned renovations, repairs, and improvements have been fully completed.
terms.formula: ARV = Current Purchase Value + Value of Renovations (determined by comps)
terms.importance: The foundational anchor for short-term fix-and-flip underwriting. Most hard money lenders cap total exposure at 70% to 75% of ARV.

terms.definition: Prepaid interest charged by the lender at closing. Each point is equal to 1% of the total loan amount (e.g., 2 points on a $500,000 loan is $10,000).
terms.importance: Primary mechanism for hard money lenders to generate short-term yield. Usually ranges from 1 to 4 points depending on experience and property risk.

terms.definition: State-level regulations setting limits on the maximum interest rates that can be charged on loans. Hard money loans often navigate complex usury environments, utilizing exemptions for business-purpose loans or broker-originated mortgages.
terms.importance: Lenders must carefully structure entity-to-entity non-owner occupied deals to comply with or legally bypass strict personal usury limits.

terms.definition: An escrow account set up during closing containing a portion of the loan funds designated exclusively to make the monthly mortgage payments during the construction or renovation period.
terms.formula: Reserve = Monthly Interest Payment * Planned Renovation Months
terms.importance: Ensures the lender receives timely payments on pre-revenue properties, but reduces the net cash available immediately to the borrower.

terms.definition: A detailed project timeline built into the loan agreement specifying when and under what milestones portions of the construction escrow will be disbursed to the builder.
terms.importance: Prevents overpayment for incomplete work. Keeps construction milestones synchronized with capital allocations.

steps.description: Borrower submits property details, purchase contract, a comprehensive scope of work (SOW), and exit strategy. Asset viability is prioritized over personal credit scores.
Lender commissions an 'as-is' valuation and an 'as-completed' appraisal. The loan-to-cost (LTC) and after-repair-value (ARV) metrics are mathematically locked.
At closing, purchase funds are deployed, while construction/rehab capital is escrowed into a separate account reserved for milestone-based draws.
Borrower executes renovation phases. Periodic site inspections verify work completion before release of successive capital tranches.
The final stage where the borrower either sells the renovated asset or refinances into a long-term DSCR/traditional loan, fully paying off the hard money balance.

tips.action: Always align with sub-contractors that draws are paid upon verification, not prior. Lenders will not release funds for raw materials sitting on-site without installation.
Many lenders hold back 10% of each draw request until the final walk-through is approved. Ensure your liquid reserves can absorb this structural holdback.
Avoid creating a schedule with 20 tiny draws, as inspection fees (often $150–$300 each) will eat into margins. Consolidate into 4 to 6 macro-milestones (e.g., framing, dry-in, MEP, finishes).

strategies.tactic: If you have a proven track record of 5+ successful exits in the last 24 months, demand a reduction in origination points (e.g., negotiating 2.5 points down to 1.5 points).
If your speed-to-market is rapid, negotiate the removal of minimum interest requirements (guaranteed interest periods). A 3-month minimum interest clause can destroy profitability on a fast flip.

Always secure pre-negotiated loan extension options (typically 3 to 6 months) at inception. It is far cheaper to pay a 0.5% extension fee up front than to face default rates if project timelines slip.
